# Prospa Content Guidelines

_A comprehensive guide for creating clear, consistent, and user-centered content_

## Introduction

Thoughtful content design is at the core of creating great user experiences. Storytelling is essential to building elegant user journeys and relating to customers in a way that is straight up human. Prospa's unique approach to writing good copy is to be concise, maintain consistency and use language that is simple, engaging and human.

These guidelines provide direction for copywriters, designers, marketers, and anyone else composing copy for Prospa.

# Core Principles

_Our copy is clear, accessible and written by humans, for humans_

## Clear and Concise

Good copy is precise, simple and specific to its objective. Users should be able to quickly discern what is required of them and take action. Language should be concise and purposeful, with unnecessary words removed to prevent the message from being misinterpreted or obscured.

**Key requirements:**

- Be direct about what you want the user to do
- Lead with the highest-priority information (usually the objective)
- Keep sentences brief and avoid long blocks of text
- Use recognisable graphics/icons to help communicate meaning
- Avoid double negatives (e.g. can't not, not uncommon)

## Simple and Human

Our users are human, just like us. Speaking to users in a way that feels real and not robotic instils trust in our expertise without having to use overly complex or technical language. Simple verbs, first/second person and active voice indicates relatability and responsibility, and keeps user goals in focus.

**Key requirements:**

- Use verbs in their simplest forms (e.g. use "get" not "obtain")
- Primarily use first/second person (e.g. you, your, we, our)
- Favour active voice, where the subject of the sentence performs the action (e.g. 'you sent an email' instead of 'an email was sent by you')
- Avoid formal language and terms that are too complex or technical
- Maintain a positive tone

## Keep it Consistent

Content should be consistent in tone, structure and style to maintain clarity and create a cohesive brand voice across the product. However, consistency needs to be contextually relevant; in the instance that being consistent could lead to user confusion, always favour understanding over uniformity.

**Key requirements:**

- Maintain consistency in sentence structure, tense and person
- Follow guidelines for our approach to grammar and punctuation
- Use consistent wording, especially for product/feature names
- Favour user understanding if consistency could result in confusion
- Refer to Prospa's brand voice guideline for additional direction on tone

## Context is Key

Context dictates how the other principles should be adhered to at specific moments in the product journey. Knowing what users need to know, when they need to know and how it should be communicated is vital in creating thoughtful and relevant copy. Providing context also helps the user understand why we require them to perform particular actions.

**Key requirements:**

- Write copy in situ to understand how it interacts with design elements
- Drip-feed information when it is most relevant
- Know when users will require more information/explanation/instruction
- Use tool tips to define complex concepts
- Where necessary, be transparent about why we require a certain action

## Always Accessible

Our users represent a diverse range of demographics, backgrounds and experiences. To ensure equal access to our products, our content strives to demystify complex financial processes while meeting current accessibility standards as outlined in Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1.

**Key requirements:**

- Avoid technical financial jargon in favour of simple language
- Always user test copy where possible
- Use ARIA roles and attributes to provide additional context or instructions for screen readers and other assistive technologies
- Ensure all images have alt text (alternative text that describes what the image is depicting or communicating)
- Refer to WCAG 2.1 for latest accessibility recommendations

# Style Guide

_Our unique approach to language style and structure conveys who we are_

These style basics form the fundamental building blocks of any content written for our products. Adhering to these structure and styling rules will ensure any content you create looks and sounds like Prospa.

## Use Sentence Case

We almost exclusively adhere to sentence casing (i.e. capitalising the first word of the sentence only), including in headings and subheadings.

**Do:**

- Make business happen
- Good afternoon, Lottie

**Don't:**

- Make Business Happen
- Good Afternoon, Lottie

Title case is only used for proper nouns (e.g. names, roles/titles, company names) or when specifically referencing Prospa products. Title case is not used for product features (e.g. pay anyone, account settings) unless otherwise specified.

When using title case, don't capitalise articles (e.g. a, the, of) unless they are at the beginning of the sentence.

**Do:**

- Download the Prospa App
- Close your line of credit and apply for a new Prospa Line of Credit
- Update in your account settings

**Don't:**

- Download the Prospa app
- Close your Line of Credit and apply for a new Prospa Line Of Credit
- Update in Account Settings

## Favour Active Voice

Favour active voice as it is more direct, conversational, and better conveys who is responsible for a particular action. Active voice means that the subject of the sentence performs an action rather than the subject having an action done to it (passive voice). It often looks like this:

Subject (person/thing), verb (the action), object (receives the action)

Words like "was" and "by" could indicate you're writing in passive voice.

**Do:**

- You submitted a payment
- We're still processing your application

**Don't:**

- A payment was submitted
- Your application is still being processed by our team

### Lead with the Objective

Copy should almost always begin with the highest priority information. This often means starting a sentence with the user objective or goal, rather than the UI action we require them to make.

**Do:**

- To create a transaction report, enter start and end dates below.

**Don't:**

- Enter start and end dates below to create a transaction report.

### Using Passive Voice

Passive voice may be used in instances when it is more concise, usually in microcopy (e.g. buttons, navigation items) where the subject is implied or when it is more important to emphasise the action over the subject.

**Do:**

- Changes saved

**Don't:**

- We saved your changes

## Use Personal Pronouns

Using first-person and second-person pronouns humanises both us and the user, but it is important to know when each is applicable. Pronouns are always gender-neutral, unless talking about a specific person.

### Second-person Pronouns

Second-person pronouns (you, your) are used to reference our users, especially when providing guidance or explaining an action the user is required to take. It also helps convey user ownership and/or responsibility.

**Do:**

- Enter your details
- Your card will arrive by mail
- Search for your business address

**Don't:**

- Enter details
- Cards are sent by mail
- Search for my business address

### First-person Singular Pronouns

First-person singular pronouns (I, my) are used to reflect the user's point of view, usually within actionable elements like buttons, links, checkboxes and radio buttons. It is especially important to use these pronouns to convey personal responsibility when granting consent or accepting legal terms.

First- and second-person pronouns should not be mixed.

**Do:**

- I understand
- I consent/I agree

**Don't:**

- You understand
- You consent/you agree
- To see my latest statements, log into your account

### First-person Plural Pronouns

First-person plural pronouns (we, us, our) are used to reflect Prospa's point of view. These pronouns help the user to understand when the onus is on us to complete a process or perform an action. They also help to convey the human processes behind our technology.

**Do:**

- We're still processing your application
- We can't help you at this time

**Don't:**

- Your application is still being processed
- Prospa can't help you at this time

## Favour Present Tense

We favour present tense as it feels more interactive and is usually more concise. However, simple past and future tenses can also be utilized if more context needs to be given about when an action occurred or should occur.

**Do:**

- Submit application
- Your card is now active
- You'll get a call

**Don't:**

- Application will be submitted
- Your card has been activated
- We will be calling you

## Simplify All Language

The language we use is one of the most important tools we have to connect with our users. Words are precisely chosen to reflect our meaning in the simplest and most accessible way, so that all users are able to understand.

### Be Brief

Short, punchy sentences are more direct and easier to read. Long sentences that are wordy, reference multiple ideas or use a lot of commas can confuse readers. Try breaking up long sentences and/or choosing language that reflects your meaning in as few words as possible.

**Do:**

- An error occurred. Contact our support team or try again later.
- Your application is being reviewed by our credit team. We'll give you a call once they're done.

**Don't:**

- An error occurred but don't worry; you're able to contact our support team or just try again later.
- Your application is being reviewed by our credit team, so all you need to do is sit back and we'll give you a call once they're done.

### Simple Verb Forms

Use verbs in their simplest form to create conversational and digestible copy, unless the simple verb does not provide enough context. Avoid colloquialisms and verb forms that are not widely recognised.

**Do:**

- You'll get a call
- Get a quote
- Enter your details

**Don't:**

- You'll receive a call
- Obtain a quote
- Pop in your details
- Get your transactions (instead of "Sync your transactions")

### Jargon and Technical Terms

Complex financial/technical jargon and industry-specific terms should be avoided, or used only with enough context to ensure their meaning is clear to the user. This may mean sacrificing shorter copy to provide clarifying information, or utilizing tool tips if there is not enough space.

Terms that users are highly likely to be familiar with can be used (e.g. ABN, cash flow, annual turnover, etc).

**Do:**

- How long have you been trading?
- Your repayment is 4 days overdue

**Don't:**

- Time trading?
- You're 4 days in arrears
- No need to pledge collateral to securitise your loan (instead of "No need to put your house or other assets down to secure your loan")

## Use Australian English Spelling

Prospa follows Australian English spelling rules (or UK English as a fallback). Ensure your spellcheck is set correctly to avoid misspellings.

**Do:**

- Licence
- Organise
- Favour
- Labelled

**Don't:**

- License
- Organize
- Favor
- Labeled

# Common Wording and Naming Conventions

## Product Names

When referencing Prospa products, always use title case. On the first reference, we write the product name in full. For the secondary reference or in-product, use its shortened form as follows:

| Full name<br>(primary or first reference) | Shortened name<br>(second or in-product reference)                    |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Prospa Small Business Loan                | Small Business Loan                                                   |
| Prospa Business Loan Plus                 | Business Loan Plus                                                    |
| Prospa Business Line of Credit            | Business Line of Credit                                               |
| Prospa Business Account                   | Business Account                                                      |
| Prospa Visa Business Debit Card           | Business Debit Card (in-product)<br>Prospa Card (secondary reference) |

**Do:**

- See how a Prospa Small Business Loan could take you further
- In-product: See all transactions in your Business Account

**Don't:**

- See how a Prospa small business loan could take you further
- In-product: See all transactions in your Prospa Business Account

## Platform Names

When referencing Prospa platforms, always use title case. Platforms may be known by different names internally than what they should be referenced as externally. Correct wording of Prospa platforms are as follows:

| External name         | Internally known as                            |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Prospa Online         | Customer Web Portal<br>Business Account Portal |
| Prospa App            | Mobile App                                     |
| Prospa Partner Portal | Partner Portal                                 |

**Do:**

- Log in to Prospa Online
- Download the Prospa App now

**Don't:**

- Log in to the Customer Portal
- Download Prospa's mobile app now

## Features

Referencing features within the Prospa product may be different to how it is referenced in-market. Below are the correct styling and wording when referencing features in-product:

| Do                                      | Don't                           |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Account                                 | My account, your account        |
| Bills / Bill Pay                        | BillPay, bill pay, Bill pay     |
| Help Centre                             | Help centre                     |
| Pay                                     | Pay anyone                      |
| Prospa Intelligent Quoting<br>Prospa IQ | Intelligent quoting<br>ProspaIQ |
| Settings                                | My settings                     |
| Statements                              | My statements                   |
| Tap to Pay                              | Tap to pay, Tap To Pay, TTP     |

# Voice and Tone

## Our Voice

Prospa's brand voice can be summarised in one phrase: **straight up human**. We write copy that is open, direct and keeps things simple, breaking down difficult concepts in an approachable, human way.

- **Straight up:** we get to the point using simple, accessible language and speak openly and directly to avoid ambiguity
- **Always engaging:** we provide clear, relevant details that keep users informed without inundating them with unnecessary information
- **Fully invested:** we're passionate about users' needs and use relatable language to foster connections and empower them to take control

## Tone Map

While our brand 'voice' could be described as our personality, our 'tone' is more like our mood, which changes depending on the context in which we are writing. Emulating the correct tone for each type of copy is important to ensure our message is received in the way we intend it.

### Lighthearted

- Social posts
- Content cards
- Blog articles
- Headings
- Empty states
- CVP pages
- Buttons
- Push notifications
- Confirmation modals

### Concise

- Toasts
- Error modals
- Tool tips
- Forms
- Banner alerts
- Labels
- Service messages
- Inline alerts
- Disclaimers

### Serious

- Disclaimers
- Service messages
- Inline alerts

# Writing for Components

## Banner Alerts

_Draw attention to information the user needs to know_

Banner alerts serve a number of functions, but as a whole they help draw the user's eye to important information that they may need to consider or understand, often before they proceed with an action.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Keep copy brief, only provide context if necessary
- Use full sentences
- Alerts may include an optional CTA in the form of linked text
- Etiquette can be used in the case of banner errors or when asking the user to perform an action

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Favour active voice
- Choose the correct banner colour for the banner type (see below)
- Keep alerts to 1-2 sentences maximum
- No end punctuation is required unless the alert is two or more sentences long (or one sentence with multiple clauses)

**Banner Types:**

- **Green:** indicates a success or a confirmation of an action
- **Blue:** represents important insights and neutral alerts
- **Yellow:** provides a warning to the user
- **Red:** an error or issue has occurred
- **Grey:** primarily used for promotional purposes

## Buttons

_Actionable components that put the user in control_

Buttons set user expectations by clearly and succinctly outlining the action or outcome that will occur once they are selected. They guide users and ensure they feel in control of their journey.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Keep copy concise and the instruction predictable
- Structure is usually verb + noun (e.g. Explore products, Submit application, Email bill) or a simple action (e.g. Okay, Cancel, Edit)
- Don't overuse buttons; ensure there is only one primary button per page

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Ideally three words or less
- Avoid end punctuation (unless it's a question)
- Primarily use present tense
- Drop articles (e.g. a, an, the) and pronouns (e.g. we, our, your, my, I) unless they are required for clarity

## Headings and Subheadings

_Short, scannable copy that guides the user through the journey_

Headings and subheadings help users quickly scan and absorb the most important concepts or instructions on any given screen. They are the primary way in which we guide users through journeys and an important tool in effective storytelling.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Need to be concise and scannable
- Outline the main action, instruction or contents of a page
- Create hierarchy; highest-priority information should be first/largest
- Tell a story; headings reflect the user journey and change depending on what information they require most at each step in the flow

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Use single sentences and keep them brief
- Try to keep headings to a few words; subheadings can be longer
- Avoid punctuation (unless it's a question or exclamation)
- Use actionable language where applicable and favour present tense

## Inline Alerts

_Highlighting errors and providing instruction in forms and inputs_

Inline alerts (also known as inline errors) appear beneath input fields where data entered by the user is invalid or missing.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Copy highlights what the user must do to rectify the error (e.g. Enter an amount above 1, or Enter a valid email address)
- Copy is limited to a few words, unless additional context is required
- Etiquette is not required, unless an error has occurred on our end or because we did not initially provide enough information

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Text appears in red
- Don't use end punctuation unless copy is two or more sentences

## Labels

_Microcopy used in checkbox, radio button and form components_

Labels are short, descriptive pieces of microcopy used to identify and explain the purpose of interface elements like radio buttons, checkboxes, and form fields.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Labels should be concise—ideally only a few words—and designed to fit the space provided
- Etiquette is not required
- A group of checkboxes, radio buttons or form fields may include a 'group label' that concisely states the category of the group or describes the action required by the user

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Long labels wrap to a second line; never truncate with an ellipsis
- Labels don't require end punctuation, except in the case of standalone checkboxes asking for consent
- Indicate which inputs are optional by including (Optional) at the end of the label

## Modals

_Message overlays for confirmations, errors, announcements and more_

Modals are UI elements that appear on top of the main content on the screen to communicate additional information such as confirmations, errors, feedback, additional information, or announcements.

### Specifications

**Modals can be used for:**

- **Errors:** that need more detail than inline alerts or banners can offer
- **Confirmations:** that provides extra information a user might need before they proceed
- **Announcements:** for new features, products or improvements
- **Feedback:** measures user's experiences, primarily at the end of a flow
- **Additional information:** like FAQs or details that don't fit on the page

**Styling:**

- **Heading:** outlines what the user needs to know at a glance
- **Body text:** provides context in 1-2 sentences with proper punctuation
- **Button (optional):** directs the users to a desired action
- **Iconography/imagery (optional):** adds interest or supports the copy

## Toasts

_Providing confirmation and feedback on user actions_

Toasts, also known as snackbars, provide confirmation feedback to the user that an action they performed is occurring or has occurred. They appear as a brief text modal that temporarily pops up at the bottom of the user's screen.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Keep copy to a minimum, no more than a few words
- Copy provides a clear confirmation of the user's action
- Celebratory language or etiquette is not required
- Toasts may or may not include a link or action button

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- Use personal pronouns to indicate ownership (e.g. your bill)
- Favour active voice, but use the appropriate tense to indicate when the action occurred/will occur
- No punctuation is required, however an ellipsis can be used to indicate an action that is currently occurring (e.g. downloading...)

## Tool Tips

_Adding more context without taking up additional space_

Tool tips are used to provide additional information, such as a definition or explanation, in the case that the user may not fully understand a word or phrase in the context it's being used.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Copy is concise, usually no more than one short sentence
- Use simple language to ensure comprehension; avoid jargon
- Etiquette is usually not required

**Styling:**

- Use sentence case
- No end punctuation is required unless the tool tip is two or more sentences long

# Copy Matrix and Approved Content

## Service Messages

_How to communicate updates and urgent messages to users_

Service messages are delivered to users when there are important updates or urgent information they need to know about. Service messages may utilize push notifications, emails, banner alerts and/or in-app messages.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Copy must be succinct while capturing all the necessary details
- Be specific about the situation/problem, especially in regard to time frames
- Use simple terms; avoid jargon and technical language
- Use etiquette to indicate responsibility (i.e., if the user is inconvenienced due to an issue or action on our end)

### Components

- Banner alerts (red or yellow)
- In-app messages
- Push notifications
- Emails
- Service updates page

## Disclaimers

_Clear and concise information the user should consider before proceeding_

Disclaimers provide important information the user needs to consider before they proceed with an action, especially when those actions are irreversible. They are also used when consent needs to be collected or may provide a snapshot of the terms and conditions users are agreeing to by continuing.

### Specifications

**Key requirements:**

- Copy should be clear and specific
- Disclaimers can vary in length depending on the level of detail required but should always be concise and to-the-point
- Use full sentences and proper punctuation to avoid misinterpretation
- Etiquette can help to stress the importance of the disclaimer (e.g., please double check the details)

---

_Don't forget to double check the details—if you make a mistake we might not be able to fix it!_
